utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Everyone seems to be here. Yes. Prosecution is Mr. Thayer together with Mr. McCloskey, lead counsel. All right. So good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You are a Prosecution witness, and before you start your testimony, you need to enter a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of this solemn declaration. Once you have read it, that will be an undertaking, a solemn undertaking that you will have made with us to testify the truth. So, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's going to happen is Mr. Thayer will be referring to your previous testimony in another case, giving us a summary of what you testified in that other case, Blagojevic case, and Jokic. And then we will proceed with some questions. He will then be followed by cross-examination from the various Defence teams. We'll make an effort to try and finish your testimony today, if possible. If not, you will come back again tomorrow. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, good morning. I'm going to hand you a sheet of paper with the assistance of Madam Usher. I would just ask you to read it to yourself and just confirm that your name is written above the number PW-133. And, for the record, this is P02334.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, before I begin asking you some questions about your prior testimony, I just wanted to confirm some general biographical information for which we will not need to go into private session. I'll be general enough about it. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what year you were born in, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Shall we do this in open session or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm keeping it general enough, so I think we can remain in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why -- I heard what you had said earlier but I tried to give you a hint. So let's redact this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to be safe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, have you had an opportunity to review your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Getting there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did one of our language assistants, sir, read to you your testimony in the Krstic and the Blagojevic cases?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention specifically to your testimony in the Blagojevic case. Was that entire testimony read to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you attest before the Trial Chamber that that testimony which was read to you was a fair and accurate transcription of the testimony which you gave in the Blagojevic case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to turn your attention to a summary I'm going to read of that testimony, and I just ask you to listen as I summarise it, and at the end if there are any additions or corrections that you'd like to make, you'll have an opportunity to do so, okay? The witness became a ham radio enthusiast at the age of 17 or 18. He really liked it and eventually obtained a category B licence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we may move into private session just for a couple of paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The witness did the same job at his location as he did at the other location and both locations used similar or the same equipment. His location was a higher elevation than the other location and the received signal was clearer. Other factors that affected the quality of the signal included the direction in which the antennas were pointed, or was pointed, whether the phones and antennas of the participants were facing the operator's location, the make of the antenna and the weather. At his location, the established procedure was thus: They had several receivers receiving signals from radio relay 800 and radio relay 1. They also had scanners which were always on and were used to scan various frequencies. Sometimes the scanners would stop whenever a signal appeared on a given frequency, at which time they would stop the machine and start the reel-to-reel recorder which was linked to the receiver by depressing the pause button on the recorder, record the conversation and stop the recorder or press the pause button again at the end of the conversation. In cases where he was unable to record the beginning portion of a conversation but could still hear that portion of the conversation in which the names of participants or code names were mentioned, he would immediately write that information in the notebook. Before the introduction of notebooks he would write the information on a piece of paper. It was left to their discretion to decide on the relevance of a given conversation. If a conversation was important, they would immediately rewind the tape and transcribe the conversation into a notebook. A computer operator would then type in the text, encrypt it, and forward it to their centre. If a conversation were less important, they could wait a couple of hours or so. If a conversation were unimportant, they did not transcribe it. While transcribing a conversation he wrote down exactly what he heard. If there was something he was not sure about he would place a question mark in the notebook, and if he could not hear a portion at all, he would place dots. If something were unclear to the typist, for example someone's handwriting, an error or the meaning of a sentence, the typist would ask him and he would tell the typist or replay the tape over and over again and listen, sometimes with the help of others, then tell the typist what to add. The typist's duty was to type out what the operators recorded. It was not the typist's job to change anything without the intercept operator's approval. He could not know if an intercept operator or a typist added words which may have been synonyms that changed the meaning of a sentence. That would have been perfectly possible. The witness recognised an intercepted conversation in his handwriting contained in an original notebook from his location. He identified the participants as Colonel Ljubo Beara and General Krstic by recognising Krstic's voice, by the two participants using their names when speaking to each other, and by the frequency on which Krstic was communicating, which they had programmed into their equipment since Krstic was a very important figure in the VRS at the time and they often listened to him. He did not write the date of the conversation down but he could say that it occurred on either the 14th or 15th of July, 1995, based on a reference in the conversation to 13 July and to the date of 16 July 1995 written on the last page of the conversation in his handwriting. He also bases this conclusion on the heading of the printout of the conversation which bears the date of 15 July 1995. He then identified some differences between his handwritten transcription of the conversation and a typed version of the same conversation. For example, at first in the notebook he wrote, "Tasic or Sladojevic." Because that is what he heard in the beginning of the conversation. Later in the conversation he heard the names "Nastic" and "Blagojevic," so he wrote those names down. By the time the conversation was typed from the notebook to the printout, the reference to Tasic or Sladojevic was corrected to Nastic or Blagojevic. In addition, the printout included two words which were not in the notebook. He identified some other differences between the notebook and the printout but the sense or meaning of the sentence stayed the same. The missing words were not so important and leaving them out sped up the work. He then identified notebooks and/or printouts of the same conversation as intercepted and transcribed by two other units, including the other location. The witness then recognised a second intercepted conversation in his handwriting contained in a notebook. He identified the participants as Krstic and Obrenovic because they introduced themselves and called each other by name. It was also not difficult to recognise Krstic's voice. He noted the time and day in the notebook but not the date. When shown the typewritten version of the conversation, which bears the date of 2 August 1995, he concluded that that was the date that was entered by the encryption officer while he was typing it so that meant that the officer typed it that day, encrypted it and sent it to their centre. Based on that, he concluded that that was the day the conversation took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, that concludes the summary. Based on what I just read, are there any corrections or additions which you would care to make?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I think that that is all very well done. I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With the assistance of Madam Usher, I just want to hand you an item. Sir, it's a packet containing material pertaining to three intercepts which is being handed to you by Madam Usher. In preparing for your testimony today, did you review certain material in that packet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And specifically does the packet contain handwritten transcriptions of three intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you recognise the handwriting of those three transcriptions, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes. That's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did I also show you three original intercept notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And without identifying any locations by name, sir, can you tell the Trial Chamber where those notebooks came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: The notebooks are from the location where we were doing the intercepting work.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And sir, were you able to identify in those notebooks your original handwritten transcriptions which are copied into that packet before you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And are the photocopies that are contained in the packet fair and accurate reproductions of your original notebook entries, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in addition to your handwritten entries, does the packet contained typewritten daily reports or printouts of those three intercepted conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, did you have an opportunity to compare the typewritten documents with your handwritten entries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber whether or not those typewritten versions are in fact the reports or printouts created from your handwritten notebook entries?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic, what's the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the objection is that this witness is not the witness or there is no foundation that he typed the material and we know from previous witnesses that they're not analysts, so for him to make a comparison to contrast and to somehow give credence either to the typed version, I thought this witness was to testify just on his notes, not on the typewritten version, and then to tell us whether he thinks it's accurate or to share the differences. I think the typist or the person who typed them out can come in and then they can show us what they typed and how they felt it was different. I object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is number 2 question, number 1 being, sir, did you have an opportunity to compare the typewritten documents with your handwritten entries, and he said yes. And then the next question, which is a logical sequence to the previous one, and can you tell the Trial Chamber whether or not those typewritten versions are in fact the reports or printouts created from your handwritten Nikolic entries. So basically he's being asked to confirm whether they faithfully reproduce what he had himself written in the notebook. This is how, if we need, we can rephrase the question, but at the end of the day, second question follows the first one. There is no point in asking him the first one without asking him the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know that in his testimony, Your Honour, as I hope you'll see during the cross, he clearly indicates that he didn't know whether it was typed, he clearly indicates he doesn't know whether it was sent out, and that's what he was asked by the Judge in the other case. So I think if counsel is going to pursue that, I think it would be fair to set that as a foundation before he suggests that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thanks for that information, but of course you can raise it with the witness on cross-examination. Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for some reason on page 11, line 21, [In English]: "Handwritten Nikolic entries."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that should be "notebook," Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nikolic. That needs to be corrected, of course, and I'm sure it will be attended to. So I suggest you rephrase the question, but basically there is no point in -- sense in putting the first question without following it up with the second. And then Mr. Ostojic can -- and others can confront him with whether and when he came to know about these typewritten versions. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honour, it's a very simple question. I'll try to break it down even further.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, when you were shown the typewritten versions, can you describe to the Trial Chamber the process that you underwent when you compared the notebook to the typewritten version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're making it more complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not, Your Honour, but I don't want to waste --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not you. He is making it more complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry. Can he just tell us when instead of us having to fish it out and always be vague with the questions. If he can tell us when he met with him, when he was given the typewritten notes, and then the cross can actually be reduced to a certain degree. But we're always --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That has already been asked, if you look at line -- he's referring to when he arrived here and had meetings with, I don't know, and to a particular packet. And in addition to your handwritten entries does the packet contain typewritten daily reports or printouts of those three intercepted conversations; yes. And, sir, did you have an opportunity to compare; yes. And then what -- there was a question. So your question should only be what's your conclusion after having seen those typewritten reports upon comparing them after comparing them with your notebook entries? It's as simple as that and we move forward because we're literally wasting time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll just leave it there, Your Honour, that was I think the question that was asked and drew the objection, but that will just leave the question right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand Mr. President's question? If you need to look at the transcripts to do so --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I can say about this typed document comparing it to my handwritten document and comparing this to my recollections from that location as we did it on the computer, I can say that this resembles that document both in terms of heading and in terms of how the information was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is your conclusion, sir, after seeing that those typewritten reports upon comparing them with your notebook entries in terms of whether or not they are actually the typewritten versions of your notebook entries?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll object to the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think you need to rephrase it. I mean, just ask him what his conclusion is. After having compared the notebook entries with the printouts that you were given, what's your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My conclusion is that my handwritten version of this document resembles the other one and that the data is the same, the one that I wrote in my handwriting, and then there is the heading that we used to always put on that location on the computer, so this document resembles that format. And I can tell you that it is most likely from (redacted). I can't confirm that with 100 per cent certainty but it certainly resembles that format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's redact this part, line 13, on my monitor at least because sometimes it doesn't correspond exactly. Please don't mention the names of any of the sites again. Mr. Thayer had explained that to you in the beginning. You are using - or at least that's the interpretation that we are receiving - the word "resembles." Why are you using the word "resembles" and not is exactly the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you that my handwriting and this document are identical to some minor errors in the typed document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we may move into private session just for one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, I want to turn your attention to the conversation -- for those of us who are looking at the packets, it's at tab 1. And may we have 65 ter number 1179B, Bravo, on e-court, please? And, sir, actually if you would look on what is on your screen, tell me when you see an image, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's on your screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes. This is my handwritten cable from that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And looking at this first page, at the -- pretty much the first line there, do you have the participants to this conversation listed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes. Underneath the time and frequency, in the first line, right below that you see the names of two participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you read who those participants are, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: The first one is Colonel Ljubo Beara and the second one is General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you just referred to the frequency that is written. Can you read for the Trial Chamber what other information is listed above the participants. And for the record if you would also just read what the frequency for this conversation is, as you recorded it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: The frequency was 255.850 megahertz, and then you see the time indication of the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What is that time, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: The time is 1000. You can't see the zero very well, but I can see that it's 10.00, 1000.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And there is something written to the far right of that. Do you see what that word is, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes. In parentheses it says, Krle.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, at the time you actually intercepted this conversation, were you aware of what General Krstic's nickname was?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to interrupt, but this is all covered in the Blagojevic case which the Prosecutor is tendering as evidence. It's in the transcript, so if he's going to read the entire transcript back to us, we can thank him in advance, but I think it's a waste of time, and we would like to get out of here as soon as possible, given the breaks. And, quite frankly, he's just repeating questions that he's selecting from Blagojevic. And if he wants to read the whole transcript, he's welcome to do it, but it's all in the Blagojevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a follow-up to this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Of course I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified in Blagojevic that you were able to recognise General Krstic's voice and that your equipment was set to his frequency and that he and Colonel Beara referred to each other by name in the conversation. But I want to turn your attention to your Krstic testimony, because in Krstic you testified in a bit more detail than in Blagojevic about what I'm going to ask you. At the time you were listening to the conversation, was Colonel Beara known or unknown to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon first.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now, my colleague made an objection that we were reading over again the Blagojevic transcript which now on the record. Now we are referring to the Krstic transcript. The witness was asked whether his testimony was accurate in the Blagojevic but now we are saying no, it's more accurate in Krstic. I really don't understand where our colleague is leading us this morning. This is all on the record, Mr. President. The Prosecution is trying to do by the back door what they can't do by the front door. They've got all this on the record. Now they are asking questions over again. Maybe there is a purpose behind this, but we can't see it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unfortunately you weren't here yesterday, because yesterday the question was raised whether the Prosecution should have indeed chosen the Blagojevic testimony and ignored, according to the submission, the Krstic one, not asking to have it introduced under Rule 92 ter, and we had an open discussion on this and it was made very clear that Prosecution has a right to choose which of the two transcripts -- or, rather, has a right to restrict itself to one transcript and introducing that under Rule 92 ter if they want to. But also, it was declared at the time by Mr. Thayer, in response to what was the gist of the objection from Mr. Ostojic, that there will be questions during the examination-in-chief referring to parts from Krstic, which required some clarification. And then if anybody wishes to have the Krstic transcript introduced into the records, we intimated that we were leaving all doors open. That was what happened yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, even though I was not present in the courtroom yesterday, I do read the transcripts and I was aware of the debate that took place between my colleague and the Prosecution. However, at this time, what we are having is that we are asking questions about the Krstic transcript and that's, as was decided, not on the record. Then I will just say that the nature of my objection is to say it's a leading question. Why does he ask -- does he not ask the witness an open question about what happened and not what he said in a case that is not on the record. We are just confusing the issues this morning, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. But the problem is that it's 92 ter. It's restricted. They know what the restrictions are. They can give you both or neither or one transcript. They made a decision. Now they are trying to be selective in Krstic, and they're not telling us, although he claims that he -- whatever his question was, why doesn't he ask him why didn't you mention that in Blagojevic? Why doesn't he tell us specifically how many times he met with the Prosecutor, when was the first time that he gave notice to the Defence that actually he's going to have certain testimony here that we received the day before? Those are the questions if we are going to have a 92 ter witness and transpose him into a live witness but only summarise things for the Prosecutor, it's very unfair and it's prejudicial. If this witness -- with all due respect to the witness, if the Prosecutor wants to have a live witness, bring him as live. They suggest that he's 92 ter, and then he's repeating questions that were asked in Blagojevic. That question was asked in Blagojevic, they didn't -- the Prosecutor didn't ask the question in Blagojevic. They should live with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we covered this when we handed our decision introducing the 92 ter procedure to you for the purpose of this trial, making it clear that 92 ter procedure does not mean that you introduce the prior testimony and no questions will be asked by the Prosecutor or could be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The position again is as I tried to explain earlier. The procedure in Rule -- the Rule 92 ter procedure allows the Prosecution, after the summary, to proceed with the questions they would like to put to the witness. Now, we discussed yesterday and also today the question of the Krstic transcript, and there is no doubt that in areas which were covered in the Krstic trial that were not, according to you, covered in Blagojevic, you have every right to ask questions to the witness as per your declaration of yesterday. But it would be preferable, I suppose, not to directly refer the witness to the transcript in Krstic unless that becomes necessary as an aide-memoire to refresh his memory or to assist in his testimony. Otherwise, you can put -- you can lead on -- you can put the question -- you can put the question just the same. Try to avoid as much as possible referring to the Krstic, with the understanding that, of course, that would not apply to any of the Defence teams. The Defence teams are free to refer to the Krstic transcript in whatever manner they like. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, and my references to the actual Krstic testimony actually were designed more to facilitate understanding with my learned colleagues so that they would understand what I was doing based on our discussions yesterday. But I will heed your advice or your instruction, Your Honour, and I will not refer to that prior case in the further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour; and thank you for that, my learned colleague. But, Your Honour, the question is not accurate and we object to form as well, on page 19, line 11. It's not what he says in Krstic and he's just -- it's a misrepresentation of what's on Krstic. And I would only ask my learned colleague, for him to cite the page, because the page I'm looking at is 4472, specifically line 14, and the question actually has a different meaning than what the Prosecutor is asking now because he prefaces the question at the time "while you were listening to the conversation," and that's not what was asked in Krstic, and that's not what was ever asked by any of the interviews that this witness conducted with the Prosecutor or their investigators. It's a complete -- it's a complete bad question in form and somebody stands --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic is kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you would be able to cover that on cross-examination. What we are trying to say is that Mr. Thayer doesn't need to draw the attention of the witness to his testimony in Krstic to ask the question whether at the time you were listening to the -- he was listening to the conversation, Colonel Beara was known or unknown to him. You can put the question direct and then one draws the conclusion referring to the Blagojevic testimony and to the Krstic testimony if that is brought up at any moment by the Defence. So this is what I'm trying to convey as a message, and let's try and move forward also because Mr. Ostojic is anxious to leave as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's been a long --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, at the time you were listening to this conversation, was Colonel Beara known or unknown to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the objection now?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, the objection is that clearly on December 11 of this year, two days ago, we received a letter from the Prosecutor indicating supplemental information. The first time this was actually revealed to the Defence is in the letter, as I said, dated the 11th of December, from Nelson S. T. Thayer, Jr., Trial Counsel, and it says in that first paragraph that this is new information that is just now supposedly this witness will testify to. So I object to it. It's untimely, it was never disclosed to the Defence at any time, and it's not included in any of the materials we have from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you expect the Prosecution to disclose to you the questions that it will be asking the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not the questions, but if there is a witness that has a claim, Your Honour, specifically as to the acts or conduct of any of the accused, they are required under the rules to identify them and to produce it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Thayer, with your question. There is absolutely no foundation to your objection, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just for the record, we can discuss this, if the Court deems it necessary, out of the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Proceed with your -- please proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic has made factually incorrect statements, and I can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: -- speakers please not overlap and slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I mean -- I understand but he can't make those accusations, Your Honour. We had a discussion about it yesterday, I was clear on my point, and he obviously knew I was clear on my point, and he's a bit perturbed about it. But I would ask my learned colleague --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Ostojic please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And, please, no further arguments on this point. I do understand Mr. Ostojic's frustration with -- following your comment, which I think shouldn't have been made. All right? So let's try to keep the same environment with which we have been working throughout since we started this trial, especially today, which may be the last day before we break for the holidays. Please proceed with your question. I don't think there is anything else to discuss on the issue raised by Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, at the time you were listening to this conversation, was Colonel Beara known or unknown to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as you sit here today, sir, do you recall -- well, I'll just withdraw that question. Do you recall whether you were able at the time to recognise Colonel Beara's voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how is it that you were able to recognise Colonel Beara's voice at the time you were transcribing this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: We could recognise it because we heard it frequently. He would introduce himself as Colonel Ljubo Beara. We could hear him frequently and we could recognise his voice modulation, just like many others whose conversations we intercepted. All of us on the team knew their voice modulations and Beara was no exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as you sit here today, sir, can you recall anything at all distinctive about Colonel Beara's voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Today I wouldn't be able to do that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we may turn to page 3 of the document that we've had on the screen, please. And if you're trying to follow in English. It's 65 ter 1179A of that tab but if we -- I can put that on the ELMO but it would be preferable just to keep for now the B/C/S version on the screen so that we can have a legible copy. And again, the English translation is 1179A. And, sir, I want to refer your attention to the last entry in both versions, the English and the B/C/S. It's the last B entry. Do you see that line, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I see it under B, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you just read that line, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: "B: I don't know what to do, Krle. I'm telling you seriously there are still 3500 packages that I have to distribute and I have no solution."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, looking at that handwritten transcription, can you tell the Trial Chamber what the actual word in your language is that appears after 3500, that number 3500?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: The word is "parcels."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what does that word mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: The word "paket" in our language can mean a box or a carton or something that was packed to be sent somewhere. That's what the word "paket" means.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now if we may turn to the printout, which is 65 ter 1179E, please. And we won't need to look at the English version of this. I think the B/C/S version speaks for itself. And if we could focus towards the bottom of the document, please. Again, it's the last -- the second-to-the-last entry, the last B entry. On the printout, there, sir, do you see the word "paketa"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it appears in this version to have quotation marks around it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, as you sit here today, sir, do you have any specific recollection as to how that word "paketa" ended up with quotes around it in the typewritten version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I can assume that -- well, amongst us in the team, what we believed "paket" to mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... interrupt you, sir. I'm just asking you as you sit here today, do you have any specific recollection as to how the word "paketa" ended up with quotes around it in the typewritten version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I really cannot remember precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to turn your attention to another conversation. And this is located at tab 3. May we have 65 ter 1387A displayed on e-court, please. And if you're working with a hard copy, the English translation should be located right after that document at tab 3, and that is 65 ter number 1387B. If we may focus on the second part of the page, please. Perfect. Sir, do you recognise what's on your screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm not receiving translation. I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Neither am I. You need to repeat your question, Mr. Thayer, and he needs to repeat his answer, and we try to make sure that we get interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise what's on your screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: This is my handwriting of an intercept between General Krstic and Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you would just note for the record, sir, the information that is contained in the top two lines of this handwritten entry of yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: It says in the first line "Wednesday," and then on the second line is the frequency, 245.950, the time is 9.50, and then in the continuation it says: "Participants, General Krstic, Obrenovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you can, I'd like to turn your attention to the tenth entry, if you're counting Ks and Os on the left, again it's the tenth entry down. Do you see the line attributed to Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And rather than have me read it, if you just read it yourself out loud, please, just so we understand we are on the same -- same line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: "O - Everything is, everything is going according to plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Just to make it clear for the record, was there one everything or two everythings in that line, sir? Didn't quite come out in my translation clearly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: "We have everything, everything is going according to plan." We have another line further down: "Everything is going according to plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to stay focused on that line 10: "Everything, everything is going according to plan." Would you please read the next two entries, which would be the 11th and 12th entries if you're counting Ks and Os. Would you just read those into the record, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: 11: "K - Don't leave a single one alive." And then 12: "O - Everything is going according to plan, full stop."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd just ask you with the assistance of Madam Usher to take the stylus that's next to your computer, and would you please just circle those two lines that you read, "don't leave a single one alive" and "everything is going according to plan"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then would you read the next entry, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: "K - Way to go, chief. The Turks are probably listening. Let them listen, the motherfuckers."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now those two lines that you read and circled, specifically the ones that you circled, sir, do you remember whether or not they appear in the printout version that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I don't think that they do, the last time I looked.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's, if you would, initial with PW-133, perhaps in the bottom right-hand corner, there is some clear space, just write PW-133, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we can save the exhibit and I think we'll be done for now with that. Paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, just because it flowed rather quickly and we were trying to find it, just so the record is clear, and I think there is no problem with it, but I think this intercept, the Krstic/Obrenovic purported intercept, is from the 2nd of August, just the way it was written, and there was no date given. He just said do you recognise it, but I'm sure he'll lead him through that, but I just wanted to make that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you for that observation. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We'll get there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the printout, if we may, at 1387C, please, that's 65 ter 1387C. The English translation should follow it. That's 65 ter 1387D. And if we could scroll up just a little bit and focus on that middle portion, please. A little bit higher, please. Do you see a conversation in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is the time 0950?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber what this typewritten conversation is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: This is a typed version of the transcription that I did in the notebook by hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could just for the moment scroll up to the top of the document. Do you see a date on this report anywhere, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: The date is the 2nd of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could scroll back down please and focus on that middle portion again. I'd like you to go down ten entries, if you could just count, like we did with your notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, I've counted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you read what that line says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: "O: Everything, everything is going according to plan, full stop."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you read the next line that appears on this typewritten report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: "That's the way, boss, the Turks are probably listening, let them listen, the motherfuckers."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, between the two lines you just read on this printout, is there anything missing from them that appeared in your notebook, that you wrote in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I think that another part is missing. "Everything is going according to plan," I think in front of that there was a sentence. Let me just find it, if I can, here. I think that there was one sentence before. Yes. There was the sentence, "K - All right, kill them all, God-damn it." That's already there. Then we have: "Everything, everything is going according to plan." And then underneath that in the typed version, there is a sentence missing that says: "Don't leave a single one alive." And then we have: "Everything is going according to plan." Those two sentences are missing in the typewritten version.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, are those the two sentences that you circled a couple of minutes ago on the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, in preparing for your testimony, did you also listen to a CD recording of a conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as you listened to the recording, did I ask you to try to simultaneously read your handwritten transcription and compare what you were hearing to your handwritten notebook entry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber whether you were able to identify the conversation on the CD, whether you were able to make any connection between the conversation on the CD and what you had transcribed in your notebook that we have been discussing here at tab 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was your conclusion, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: The conclusion is that it's the same intercept as the one that I transcribed. There are some minor things missing that I noticed, that I had written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At this time may we play 65 ter 1387G, please. And actually before we do that, there are a couple of ways we can deal with the translations. There is a B/C/S transcript and an English transcript. I can put one on the screen and one on the ELMO, or -- we can put the English on the ELMO, for example, and the B/C/S speakers can just listen to the tape, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember how we did it the last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Last time we did nothing, Your Honour. I think we just played it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- but that was a response to a specific request that we should hear the conversation without any interruptions or any translation or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I agree, Your Honour. And I was just suggesting to simply put it on the ELMO so people could read along without any simultaneous translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear what Mr. Ostojic has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Although the Zepa issue doesn't concern us directly as such, Your Honour, we adopted a procedure to hear it. We've objected in the past to the English translations. We continue to make the objection. Also I think it's important for the Chamber to know that there is other evidence even from an expert, Dr. French, that the Prosecutor had that gave an opinion on this tape. I don't want to share it. I think it's their obligation to share it for a fair proceeding. And I also think the position of General Krstic on this is important as well, which he had a position on, which was perhaps similar to Dr. French. Now, this witness can say whatever he wishes and believes. I think we should just listen to the tape or not have the either English version or the OTP's typed out version of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we -- it's the classical case of trying to hit two birds with one stone. In the first place, I think we need to observe the same rule that we introduced last time when we heard something similar; namely, that it should be heard without any other sound being piped through, but then, I mean, everyone, I think, needs to know what is that recording supposed to be saying. So we need to see on the monitor at least the -- what you purport to be the English transcript of the conversation, leaving of course all matters relative to that unprejudiced. But we need to be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, these are in everybody's packets so they can be followed in hard copy as well, in addition what we have on the ELMO. So hopefully we'll have all bases covered for all languages. And it should be the last two documents in the packet, with the B/C/S first, I believe, and English second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just want to make sure everybody is ready to proceed. I see shuffling. We are ready whenever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we may have that conversation played, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not hearing anything. I don't know about others.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suggest unless we can resolve this in the next 30 seconds we have a break coming up, we can resolve the technical issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't hope you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I suggest we take a break now if we can, Your Honour, to resolve the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need a 30-minute break, as I explained earlier, because of the redactions. Could I ask the Defence teams to liaise with our registrar, Madam Registrar, to indicate more or less the time you require for your cross-examinations, respective cross-examinations, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that one of you or more would like to raise an issue. Yes, Ms. Condon?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I wonder Your Honour, if the courts would grant me an indulgence to make a brief oral motion. It concerns -- there is currently on behalf of the Popovic, Beara, Nikolic, Borovcanin and Pandurevic teams, there is going to be a motion filed in response to this Honourable Trial Chamber's decision on the 6th of December that concerns the decision in relation to the amendment to the 65 ter list, Your Honour, and the addition of a number of witnesses. As it currently stands, the motion is beyond the word limit that's prescribed according to the rules of this Tribunal, and as I understand the practice direction of the 16th of September, 2005, Article 7, we have to make a submission based on the fact that there is exceptional circumstances for it to exceed the 3.000 word limit. Your Honour, essentially they are these, that the motion does descend into quite a lot of detail, not superfluous detail obviously in our view, in relation to ICTY -- this Tribunal's jurisdiction and the jurisdiction of the ICTR, and as a result, it's currently -- I think it stands at 4.300 words, so it's some a thousand over the limit. So I make that application that we propose to file the motion today, but we do so in circumstances where it's currently over the limit and seek a ruling from the Trial Chamber that we can file it in that form. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the response is, it's Christmas, permission granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Especially since you are not exceeding it by inconsiderate measures, so permission granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anything else that you would like to raise? None? Let's bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, can we proceed with the audio?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We may, Your Honour. I think we have resolved the technical difficulties. And if we may play 65 ter 1387G, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By the way, the witness ought to know that it is probably not possible with -- to finish with his testimony today. I mean, I -- particularly since the Beara team requires two hours so -- but if you can reduce that we can possibly make it. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't remember if you did indicate the -- any reference number in relation to this audio. No, it's 65 ter 1387.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, G.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: G. And audio T 0000822; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, a little while ago, you read and circled two lines which were in your notebook but not in the printout, Krstic is saying, "Don't leave a single one alive" and Obrenovic saying, "Everything is going according to plan." Were you able to hear those two lines just now, as you listened to the recording?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And turning your attention to that portion of the conversation, did you hear anything on the recording which was not in your handwritten notebook entry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber some examples of what you heard but did not write down in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Well, if I remember well, I know that I didn't write down the introductory part where they say "hello, hello," where they are being connected through the switchboard, and generally I did not record such things. That's -- I wanted to record the important things. That's what I was aiming at. And then there were additional minor words such as "all right" or "hello" or "we'll be in touch" or "we'll speak later," I did not consider these things important. That's why I omitted them. And the only sentence that is missing from the written text is the one that I heard that is missing from the written text. Otherwise it's the same conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You just referred to some missing text or conversation that you heard. Do you recall, as you sit here as having just listened to that, what that missing section is that was not in your notebook but that you just heard? And if we need to look at the transcript to help identify that, please do so. Is it still on the screen in B/C/S? If you-- turning to your packet -- I'll just make this simpler. Turn to your packet, sir, the last tab, tab 3, there should be a B/C/S translation of the intercept that you just listened to, an actual translation. Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could scroll up just a little bit, is there -- is there -- and just -- is there a portion of this transcript that was not in your notebook? Does this help you recall what you heard that was not in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: This thing at the top, can we go back to the top? Can we scroll up? What I heard is this: Just a moment. And then we lost the connection with the switchboard. And then Krstic says "hello," and then that's what I didn't write down, even though I heard it on the tape. I started from this moment when Obrenovic speaks and then Krstic speaks again. So that's the portion that's omitted that I did not transcribe. And then can we scroll down, please, towards the middle? Yes? The sentence that was missing from the typewritten text is "don't leave a single one of them alive." It's here but not in the typewritten text. And then -- and then I omitted the question mark. And then I also did not record this sentence that is repeated, "don't leave a single one of them alive." I generally, as a rule, did not record repeated sentences because I did this in haste and I wanted to save time, so that's why I generally did not record this. Everything else is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. You referred to a question mark. If we are looking at the B/C/S translation, can you identify what you were referring to, and if it helps to count the Ks and Os going from top to bottom, to help identify the precise section of this transcript that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Could you zoom out so that I can count the lines. Yes. In this typewritten version or whatever it is, first it goes X and then colon and then: "Just a moment," I don't have it there. And then: "O: We lost the connection with the switchboard," I don't have that. And then Krstic says: "Hello," I don't have it in my version. And then O says: "Yes." And then Krstic says: "It's Krstic, hello," I don't have that either. And then Obrenovic says: "Yes." And then from this moment on, when Krstic says: "Obrenovic, I'm recording from there on. But, for example, I omitted Krstic is here. And then they are greeting each other, and I have that recorded. And they are speaking of their health, well, it wasn't terribly important for me either but I did record that. All right. And then they say: "Don't leave a single one alive, kill them all." No. We've come to line number 21. Line 21, in the typewritten version.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What is that line, sir, just so we're clear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: When K says: "Kill them all, God-damn it." In my version, that's line 9 because I omitted certain things. And then they say: "Everything, everything is going according to plan." That's fine. And then: "Don't leave a single one alive." Yes, that's the same as in mine. And then I omitted this yes, where Obrenovic says yes. And then he repeated on the tape: "Not a single one must be left alive." I didn't record that because I did not want to repeat the same sentence. And then the next one is all right and the next one is all right. And then all right again. And then O says: "He went up towards you." That's fine too. Can I see the next page in the typewritten version? And then they say: "When today" and then I omitted the word "yes," or "really." And then the next one is all right. And then I recorded "this morning," and then I omitted "yes." And then he says: "Go on, we'll be in touch." I omitted the word "lets." I didn't think it important because it didn't change the meaning of the sentence. Whatever did not affect the meaning of the sentence, I omitted. And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there, sir. I didn't mean for you to go through the entire conversation but I thank you for that. Other than the examples that you gave, were there any other words or conversation that you heard listening to this tape that weren't in your notebook or in the transcription which you believe alter the meaning in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: No. I didn't find that. It did not affect the meaning. The meaning was not lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to -- just my last question. I reviewed the -- your testimony from before the break, and there was one question and answer that appear just a little bit unclear in the answer, so just to clarify the record I want to ask you the question again. And that's at page 25, line 15. I asked you the question: "Sir, at the time you were listening to this conversation," and we were referring to the first conversation we discussed between Colonel Beara and General Krstic, the question I asked was: "Sir, at the time you were listening to this conversation, was Colonel Beara unknown -- I'm sorry, was Colonel Beara known or unknown to you," and your answer was yes. And that -- as I read it, is a little ambiguous so I'm just asking you if you can clarify your answer to that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Well, yes. His voice was familiar to me. I knew his name, although I did not know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I don't have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Thayer. I take it that the Popovic team is going first? Okay, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think we agreed I would go first, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. There is an agreement, so I think the Beara team then, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to put you in the picture, with the time left, we have -- I have an indication that the Popovic team will take 30 minutes, Beara two hours, the Nikolic team 20 minutes, the Borovcanin 15 minutes, and the Miletic 15 minutes, and the other two indication is that you will not need to cross-examine the witness. So that brings us to three hours 20 minutes. I don't know, we are -- yes, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to address the Chamber. We will probably have two questions only and it won't take more than five to ten minutes, and there is a chance that we won't put any questions at all, in case what we are interested in is covered by some other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very kind of you to note that, thank you. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... perhaps we can start with your familiarity with the voice of Mr. Beara. Can you tell me, sir, how often you heard his voice in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: In 1995, one could hear it frequently, not only on one channel but on several other channels, one could hear his voice. Some conversations were not important so we did not record them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. But of the ones that you recorded, do you know how many are in your book, in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, when you met with the Office of the Prosecutor did you try to go through the books a little bit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I went through the material that was in my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, to the best of your recollection, did you pick out any purported conversation that you intercepted where Mr. Beara was involved in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I didn't pay attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, how many times did you meet with Mr. Thayer or the Office of the Prosecutor in preparation for your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I would have to check that and I would need to have more time because I was here two weeks ago, then I went home, then I came back again, so I wouldn't be able to give you the exact number. I met with him at least on five occasions, at least, but I would need to verify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fair. And I'm sure we could get that from my learned colleague. Sir, can you tell us when the first time it is that you told the Office of the Prosecutor or its investigators that you were familiar with Mr. Beara's voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Once again, the question is such that I can't give you a very specific answer because I generally don't pay attention to the time and date when I'm meeting with somebody. I really wouldn't be able to help you there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose you can tell us whether this happened during this last recent occasion since you have arrived this time to give testimony here, this last week. Or whether you had made that statement before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the past week, yes, I said that. I stated that. I don't know how many times. And I think that I even said that previously, because that's a fact that is true, at the time I used to recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, tell me if you recall ever telling the investigator Stefanie Frease in 1999 when you met with her that you were familiar with Mr. Beara's voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I know that when giving my last statement, I wasn't able to recall that, but in this last period, yes, I know that I definitely told her that. But the statement before that is a bit unclear in my mind. I remembered the name and everything but I couldn't remember the content of the text. But when Stefanie Frease came I could remember, yes, then. And then several years passed and then this was not something that I tried to remember because now that I'm living a civilian life, just an everyday life, I don't try to remember things. You know, once I leave these premises I just forget everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have your information report from Stefanie Frease from 1999. No where does it mention that you told her that you were familiar and had purportedly had heard Mr. Beara's voice frequently. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Well, yes, if that's how it was then, I gave my answers at the time as I remembered, and then I guess several years later, some other recollections come to the surface, or somebody tells me something, and well, I can't really explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what you mean if somebody tells you something. Like, for example, if Mr. Thayer or someone from the Office of the Prosecutor reminds you that you remembered someone's voice, is that what you're talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: No, no, not that. Not that. It's just that if I take again the document that I wrote, if I try to cast my mind back to those days, I knew that I could recognise his voice at the time. When Stefanie Frease came to see me for the first time, I naturally couldn't remember the exact timbre of his voice, but I told you then that at the time when we were at that elevation, I could clearly and easily recognise his voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And she just failed to put that in the information report in 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I apologise. What is it that she did not put in?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That you recalled Mr. Beara's voice.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I don't know what she put in. I don't even remember that conversation now, to tell you the truth. It was a long time ago. So I can't say anything very specific about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, in preparation for your testimony, I understood that you had not only gone through it with Mr. Thayer and a translator. Did you also go through the information report of 1999, just recently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Information report. Well, the translator read to me over 120 pages of that material. Now, you know, 120 pages, I don't know whether I can remember everything that was contained there. It was simply too much for my brain to have all of that read to me but we did cover all that material.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know in June of 2000 that you testified in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, at that time, that you did not and were not asked any questions about recognising or recalling recognising Mr. Beara's voice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I don't remember that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about the March 2001 Krstic testimony that you gave? You recall you gave testimony in Krstic in March 2001; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I know that I came here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, that in that -- March 2001 when you gave testimony that at no time do you mention that you recall Mr. Beara's voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the November 2003 Blagojevic testimony that you gave, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that I came here in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's be fair. You remember it even better than that because you just reviewed it recently, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I did go through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, as you sit here now that in the Blagojevic November 2003 testimony no where do you state that you recall Mr. Beara's voice or -- voice? I don't want to have a compound issue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: No. I don't remember. I don't remember if anybody asked me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, as you sit here now in the Blagojevic November 2003 testimony that in fact no where did you state that you recall Mr. Beara's voice frequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I don't remember stating something like that. All I remember is that at that time we did recognise his voice. The other things that happened over the years, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I don't mean to interrupt you or to be rude with this question: At this time, though, I'm not interested in what "we" remembered. I'm interested only in what you, sir, remembered. And I note in your testimony you even on page 25, line 24, state "we." I want to know from you, sir, and only you, not this "we," because I'm sure Mr. Thayer can help you there but the "we" that -- the you is what I'm interested in, not the "we." As you sit here, sir, can you tell me when it was the first time that you told the Office of the Prosecutor that you recollect Mr. Ljubisa Beara's voice and that you had heard it frequently?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think from my recollection, he has already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But he's always answered it with "we" and I'm now specifying only him. So that's the only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I suppose what he is telling you is that they worked as a team.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll hear it from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's explained during the examination-in-chief that he and his colleagues used to hear -- this is his statement -- used to hear, allegedly, Mr. Beara in conversations, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that you do not recall what, if any, distinctive feature about Mr. Beara's voice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I hate to interrupt you but he's already answered that question. It was put to him and he said no, I don't recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the transcript earlier today when your summary was read on page 5, lines 22 through 24, it states that in the spring of 1994, you were transferred to the site, which I think we are calling the southern site, if we may. Is that accurate? That it was in the spring of 1994, as Mr. Thayer read your summary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: In 1994, I was transferred to short-wave listening. That wasn't the last elevation, but the last elevation where we were working from was actually in the spring of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So when were you transferred to that last elevation, the spring of 1995, not 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you be more specific and tell us when in the spring of 1995 you were transferred to the southern location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: It could have been April, maybe March. I'm not sure about the month now, and even before, I didn't really make inquiries from people in charge about that specific date, so I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, at this southern site, sir, am I correct that there were two squads that worked there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Squad, yes, and its replacement, yes, in terms of time, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the squads were divided up and one squad was comprised of people from Kladanj, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the other squad was composed of people from Banovici; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if we can go into private session for one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you a question regarding the rules regarding safekeeping of the notebooks. Am I correct that you did not have any rules regarding the safekeeping of these notebooks, these notebooks or any other documents that you were issued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: There was a standard procedure, according to which the notebooks that were used would be left at a place, and then the commander of the squad would then take charge of these notebooks. We didn't really busy ourselves with that that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me read to you from your testimony from Krstic, 22nd of June, 2000. You were asked, I think, a similar question, and it starts on page 4467, line 25: "Did you have any rules regarding the safekeeping of these documents?" And then it goes to the next page, 4468, lines 1 and 2, but I'll read the question, sir. It says: "Did you have any rules regarding the safekeeping of these documents, these notebooks or any other documents that you were issued?" Your answer, sir, on line 2 was: "No." Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: That's exactly what I said before. There was no written rule but there was a standard practice the way I explained earlier. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall the question in Krstic asked you for written rules, did it? I'll read it again. "Did you have any rules regarding the safekeeping of these documents, these notebooks or any other documents that you were issued?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the question has been asked and he has a fair answer to the question. And whether there were any rules he explained himself and I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it goes beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's true that has been partly answered but I think the question goes a little bit beyond what was dealt with before. So please proceed, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Should I restate my question, Your Honour, or I should ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I should think so because you have already phrased it slightly differently on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, my question is that you recall in Krstic that when you were asked this question we just covered and the answer that you gave, the question wasn't limited to written rules, was it? The question in fact stated any rules.
