utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I don't really remember what you're asking me from the Krstic case, but really perhaps I can reply now how it was, how we worked. I don't remember too many things from the Krstic case. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that, I'm sure. In your summary that Mr. Thayer wrote out, he states that at the southern site, or I think he called it the other site there was "the established procedures." Let's talk about those established procedures, if you don't mind. What was the rule or the established procedure with respect to initialing or signing the conversation that you purportedly intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Let me first try to explain southern and the other location. The second location was the location where I wasn't at the beginning, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can just have the Court instruct the witness just to answer the question. He doesn't have to go to the other location. We are interested obviously in this location in July of 1995 at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Perhaps, Witness, you can restrict yourself to answering that question and forget the other location.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, sir, would you like me to restate the question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, what was the rule or the established procedure in July 1995 at the southern location with respect to initialing or signing the conversations that you purportedly intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I didn't put my initials down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there was such a rule written or oral that you were required to do so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Well, since I didn't do it, obviously I didn't think that it was something that you had to do or that it was part of the procedure. Perhaps somebody did do it, but I personally did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about the rule or the established procedures with respect to dating a conversation. Same time period, July of 1995. What were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I know of the rule that when you are typing it into the computer, you had to put the date. That was the rule. When I transcribed the intercepts from the tapes, it was normal to assume that the date was already entered in the computer so sometimes I would put it down and sometimes I would not, depending on the work and the time. But I didn't really troubled with that -- I wasn't really troubled by that because I knew that the date would automatically be entered into the computer, so I knew that that would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So did you have a rule about that or didn't you in connection with your notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I do not recall that rule. Had somebody come to me and placed a written order in front of me and said, You have to put that in, I would have done it. But I just did it the way we were used to doing based on our experience. It was important for me to have the participants, the time, the channel, sometimes -- well, we didn't really need the channels because we knew which channels we were working on. Some people put that in, some didn't. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the rule or established procedure relating to accuracy or precision?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: We had to be as precise as possible so that the sentences wouldn't lose their meaning. The most important procedure was to keep the meaning in the sentence; otherwise, why would we be doing it? I mean, we were there to do this job, so we did our best, that everything was done properly and correctly, that it had meaning. We all abbreviated it in the way we felt was possible. The way I was doing it is that I would omit certain unimportant words. The procedure was not to be wrong in the sense of the sentence or in the meaning when you were passing it on. That was the most important thing. Of course, also it was important to write in the time, the participants, because that's what was entered into the computer and that is what is forwarded then to the command or to the centre. That was important to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Am I correct, sir, that despite your efforts to be as precise as possible, there were many, many reasons why that was difficult to achieve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: There weren't many but sometimes there were reasons, yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's stick with the many. I said it twice. I'm suggesting to you, sir, that there were not just many reasons but there were many, many reasons why that was difficult to achieve, that accuracy. Would I be wrong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: There were many reasons. It's different when it's many reasons at one point in time and then when we have many reasons over a certain period of time. Sometimes there would be different reasons during different time periods. Sometimes at one moment you would have different reasons. But many reasons distributed over time and the dispatches, I cannot speak about one dispatch because I cannot say that there were too many reasons at the same time, that we would have such a case where we would have a lot of reasons in one particular case at one particular point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, help me reconcile this, then: In your testimony on the 22nd of June, 2000 in the Krstic case, you were asked this question on line 19, page 4472: "In view of the nature of the conversation, the nature of the conversation, I assume you made an effort to note down every word accurately as taped; is that correct?" Your answer, sir, under oath that appears on line 22 through 23 is as follows: "We did our best to be as precise as possible. However, there are many, many reasons why that was very difficult to achieve." Do you remember giving that testimony in Krstic, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But then and now I think the same thing. Not at one point in time. There were many reasons divided over a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, share with us, sir, what those many, many reasons were that made it very difficult for you to achieve accuracy and precision.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: It's like this: One then we'll go on. One of the reasons was that if at that point in time there was a lot of electrical discharge in the air, there was a lot of crackling, a lot of noise, that would be one reason. Another reason, for example, would be if the tape was old and mostly the tapes were old, that had been rerecorded several times, there would be a kind of hum on the tape itself, and the more often you rerecorded over a certain tape, the hum would be louder. Then there would be a third reason where a section of the tape would be damaged. It was a little damaged, so it would be very difficult to transcribe a word. Sometimes it would be impossible. Another reason would be that it was windy at that point in time and the antenna had turned to a degree from its normal position so that the signal was much worse. The fourth reason was that the side where the telephones were would change their direction, that there was another point of transfer of the telephone signals so we couldn't cover that part that was perhaps overshadowed by a hill and it was a way from us. A sixth reason, for example, was that along the line from the point where we were listening to, I could draw that very easily for you, if we were on the same line the listening point, their first antenna, and their second antenna, and this antenna was directed there, and the other one was there, and ours was directed there, then the first device would be actually receiving the signal from the back so then you would have a very bad signal or no signal almost. I could remember other reasons also, perhaps, but right now, I'm trying. I mean, if you would like to know more about technical matters, it's possible, for example --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't mean to interrupt the witness, Your Honour. I thought he paused. But go ahead, if you have something else to say. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Sometimes it would happen that at the point of transcribing a dispatch or receiving it, the device would break down. This did happen sometimes. Sometimes there would be no electricity. It was war. So then we would have to run to turn the generator on while this was being done. There were many such factors. But again, it all depended. I mean, none of -- not all of these things could happen at one point in time. As I said, there were many reasons. And this is my explanation of what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, at this southern site was there anyone who was specifically assigned to analyse these texts or handwritten purported intercepted conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: From what I know, there was nobody who was entrusted with a detailed analysis of these intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me who would then make the decision, if an intercept was urgent or priority?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Each operator, according to his conscience, would decide what was important, what we felt was important, what was not. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if it was important, would you then denote it with the word "priority" or with the word "urgent"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I personally would never do that. If something was really urgent and important, I would immediately -- actually, the guy who was typing, he was always with us, we would immediately try to type out the dispatch and send it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, you know there were daily dispatches that were sent out as well, correct, at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes. If some less important or unimportant dispatches piled up, this would be sent off again. But if something was really urgent, something that we felt was urgent, we would send it off immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of the three conversations that you have in the binder before you, do you know if any of them were marked with the denotation of being urgent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I really can't remember something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not asking to you remember back 11 years ago. I know it's a long time. Take a look at them. Did you find the word "urgent" on any of those three intercepts that are in front of you, in either the written logbook or in the typed out version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I don't see the word "urgent" in any of these and I never wrote it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about the word "priority"? Do you see that word in any of those three intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I don't see it, and I don't think that I would find it because I never used to write it out. This is my experience at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, how about the typed version that the typist typed out from your handwritten notes? If you had that communication, you would tell them something was important. Would you then expect them to write it in the typed out version? The words either "urgent" or "priority"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I did not ask him to write that down. He had his own procedure that was set by the centre and given to him, so I didn't interfere much with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll ask him that when he comes, okay, that's fair. Sir, let me ask you this: How many tapes or CDs, I think as the Prosecutor called it, how many CDs did you listen to when you were visiting with Mr. Thayer in these past - I forget what you said - few days or 15 days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I don't know how many CDs but I listened to it twice, and then it would be repeated again. So I would hear it over three times altogether. I don't know how many CDs there were altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, how many conversations did you listen to, separate and independent conversations that you listened to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I listened to this intercept between General Krstic and Obrenovic. Can I look further?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: This intercept --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That one of August 2nd between Krstic and Obrenovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, I listened to that one definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did at any time, sir, you -- did the -- at any time -- strike that. Did the Office of the Prosecutor at any time provide you with a tape which purports to bear the voice of Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Can I just look at that, please? I didn't listen to this conversation. No, I can't recall listening to it on the CD, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You're referring to the conversation that's on tab 1 in the book; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But my question might be a little broader than that. Did they have you listen to any tape -- purported taped conversation which has allegedly Mr. Ljubisa Beara's voice on it, not limiting it to just tab 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's talk about the actual procedure that you used in July of 1995 when you first as an operator heard a voice on the radio, am I correct, sir, that then you would begin recording or taping the conversation regardless of its importance; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: In case of any intercept, we would depress the pause button and then later on, if we saw that it wasn't interesting, we wouldn't -- we would erase it. Sometimes we even recorded conversations only from the middle onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, after listening to the conversation, it was then actually later when the operator had time that the conversation would be transcribed into a notebook; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: That depended on what we had decided about what was important and what wasn't. As I said to you, if it was important we would immediately give it to the operator to transcribe it. If it wasn't important, we would do it later, an hour or two or three hours later or whenever we had time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at your testimony in Krstic again, the 22nd of June, 2000. Sir, did you not -- or I'm sorry, did you, not the OTP, state in describing the procedure step by step that: "when the conversation is over, we switch off the tape recorder, take a pencil and notebook and record, transcribe the conversation that was taped on the tape." Correct? I thought I gave the page number but I'll give it just in case, 4455. It starts actually on 4454 through 4455.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: That's how we did it definitely if the conversation was important. If it wasn't important, we would wait for the channel to continue and then we would transcribe it all at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So am I correct, sir, that these logbooks or at least the notes that you have in front of you, they were not done simultaneously or contemporaneously while listening to the tape itself. They were actually written in after the conversation was over. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will. I'm not sure -- I think we maybe both said it to say it slowly, so I will do that. Thank you. Sir, in connection with these notebooks or logbooks, not specifically those that you have in front of you but a general question, am I correct, sir, given the procedure that you just described, the purported intercept conversation was not taken down simultaneously or contemporaneously while listening to the tape itself but it was done, as you say, later; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: If it was a longer intercept, then naturally that had to be done later. We couldn't do it by memory. But if it was something really short, for example, some new information was being given, then, yes. For example, if they were disclosing a new frequency or something like that, then, yes, we could do it right away, but a longer intercept, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I need to figure out, sir, how many notebooks were at this southern site. Am I correct that two people were not using two different notebooks and that at any given time only one notebook was used; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: If we had only one, then we used only one. If we had two, since we had three or four pieces of equipment, then we would use more. It depended on how many notebooks we had, how many we received from the operations centre. If we had some spare ones, then, yes; if we didn't have any spare ones, then, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me read what you said in the Krstic case on the 22nd of June, 2000, and it was a question that the Honourable Judge Wald asked you, and the question was on page 4481, line 22 through 25 and then it proceeds on the next page, page 4482, lines 1 through 5. The Honourable Judge Wald: "This leads me to a question you probably answered but I want to make sure I understood the answer. Was only one person in your unit at a time using a single notebook?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please read slower, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: "This leads me to a question you probably answered but I want to make sure I've understood the answer. Was only one person in your unit at a time using a single notebook? In other words, was only one man listening and recording in a notebook at a single time? Two people were not using two different notebooks at the same time, or were they?" Your answer, sir, was: "No." And then the Honourable Judge Wald proceeds with another question: "Just one notebook at the time, right?" Your answer: "At a given time, only one notebook." That was your testimony that you gave in question -- while being

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: one notebook that was used in July of 1995 at the southern site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I can't tell you that, how many notebooks we had, how many we used. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you remember as you sit here, sir, the period of July 5th through July 14th, 1995? Do you recall what event occurred during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Could you be more specific. Events relating to what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Relating to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Well, yes. Based on the dispatches that we transcribed, we could get a pretty good idea of what was happening down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And if I tell you that the enclave, Srebrenica, fell on or about July 10th, 1995, you would recall that, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Would you accept that as a premise in my -- for my next question, sir? Would that be okay? Let's assume that, okay? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: If I'm wrong, then everybody will know some of your answers may have been inaccurate. Fair enough?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Would you expect, sir, that the period right before the fall of Srebrenica and immediately after the fall of Srebrenica would have been when your job as an intercept operator at the southern facility would have been probably most important in order to determine what the people you were listening in on were actually planning and doing. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: We must have received something from the command, a letter or an order concerning the antennas that were used for wire-tapping, the angle, the elevation and so on. I don't know what they wanted to know at the command. I don't know that, but we definitely complied with their order. I wouldn't be able to tell you anything myself. It's not like I wanted to intercept this conversation or that conversation. It was simply followed the order, we turned antennas in the ordered direction, and we intercepted the conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at your book number 22 where some of the conversations that you noted in that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And with the Court's permission and the OTP's assistance if we could have the original book be placed on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's coming right up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then if we can, on e-court, have P02331, that was I think the -- notebook 22, be placed on e-court for everyone to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's notebook 22.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It would be P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2736 and not 2731. I don't know. I mean, I stand to be corrected, but that's the indication that I have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm just going by this outline. I'm not sure which one it is. If the Court thinks it's -- it's notebook 22, and I apologise for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's no apology needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the cover, if we can put the cover on the ELMO, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sir, we've learned some things -- if I may proceed. We've learned some things about these books over the course of the last couple of weeks. And am I correct that the date the book was delivered, specifically book number 22, is June 14th, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Whether it was delivered to our elevation? Is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Huh, I can't remember that exact date. Maybe it's something on the notebook but is not clearly visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, flip to the -- flip the first page, if you want, on your right and maybe you could find it. See it to your right, sir? No, a little further. There you go.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Could you zoom out, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: It's right there next to you, no? Okay, sir. See the lady?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, okay. The original is there if you have trouble reading the copy. Okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Okay, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: What are you interested in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I want to know when the date the book was delivered to your squad. I know it's the next page but -- it's the next page, I think, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: The cover page tells me nothing, only if I would be allowed to leaf through it and to look at the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And that's why I gave you the book, the original to your right so just leaf through it and tell me if you could determine what date it was delivered. Just turn the one page over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: May I take it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Please. Do you see it on the top left-hand corner there is some handwriting and it seems to be a date of 14 June 1995? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. The first entry in this book, sir, was made on what date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: The first entry was 03.07.95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: The time for that first entry, sir, was 03:14; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Does that mean that this conversation was captured then at 3.14 in the morning or at 3.14 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Since I didn't record it, I can't tell you. Had I recorded it in the afternoon I would have said 1514, and had I recorded it in the morning I would have said 0314. I don't know what this person had in mind when they did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: The next entry, sir, is a date of July 4th, 1995, correct, at 1342?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Just a minute. 4th of July, 1995 is the next entry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: There is two entries for the 4th of July, at 1342 and at 1750, correct, being two conversations that were captured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes. But up here, the date is in red pencil and then there is something corrected. First it said 05 and then somebody added in pencil 09.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: We'll get to that in a second. I'm really just focussing on the 4th of July. There's two conversations that I thought I saw on that book for the 4th of July. And what I'm asking you, sir, on that book that you have in front of you, the original, what is the next date after the 4th of July that there seems to be a notation of a date for an intercepted conversation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. And Usher, you need to help the witness a little bit because we can barely see what is on the ELMO. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was just going to ask for perhaps an ERN reference just so we have some clarity for the record later on, because we haven't had any identifying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So what appears on the ELMO at the moment is a page with ERN 0080-4528.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then I would like, if we could, 26 and 27. I think they are just the two prior pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And we have also seen 0080-4527. And the very first transcript on page 0080-4526.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mean the first page, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps we can go also to the first page where there is the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On the left side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, that's the other one, yes. And we also saw the page from this notebook with ERN number 0080-4525.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, sir, could we go to the page that you said there might have been a change from a 5 to a 9 which is I think 0080-4528? Thank you. Do you have that page in front of you, sir? Now, my question, though, is the prior page had July 4th written on it. This page has July 9th written on it. Can you tell us, sir, what happened to July 5th, 6th, 7th, and 8th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I can only suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. We don't want you to speculate, sir. But let me ask you this: Where do you see a change from 5 to a 9 on this Exhibit 4528? It's in the top portion; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: The only reason I ask is there is another 09-07 -- I mean dot 07 dot 95 so it's the top portion that you see that; correct? The first 9 on that page; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you know who wrote in 05.07.1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he's going to mention any names --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, but we need to warn him or caution him immediately that if at any time you are asked questions which in answering you would need to mention names of your colleagues and that location at the time, please tell us so that we go in private session. Could you answer the question, please? The question was: Do you know who may have written or who wrote 05071995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, who changed it and added the 9 over the 5? And don't give us the name but just tell me if you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, sir, from the 9th to the 11th you see the entry immediately below, 11.7.95; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: What happened on the 10th of July, 1995, according to this logbook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I don't see that anything was recorded on the 10th here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Can you just quickly, sir, turn to ERN 0080-4537 which is about seven or so pages over? In the middle of that page, sir. I'm telling you this, but we could go through it page by page, but in the interests of time this entry, 16.7.95, seems to be the next date that follows the 11.7.95 entry. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. If I can just take a look. I would say that that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, sir, why the dates of July 12th, 13th, 14th, and 15th were not recorded in that section of the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I answered that question when you asked me as to why I did not write those dates. I didn't write them because they were certain to be written in the computer, if it was done on that day, and sometimes I simply did not record the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you turn to the next page, after 16.7.95, and if you just flip through it, sir, will you agree with me that after the 16th of July 1997, there are actually dates throughout this logbook, specific -- specifically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I would have to take a closer look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: If the Court doesn't mind, if it's okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, perhaps you can help him directing him to specific pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to go through the entire notebook. It's not a problem at all, but if you have a specific page you're interested in, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Ostojic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sir, on the 16th of July, 1995, there are ten conversations. So if you just count through the conversations you'll find the next date, and as soon as I find it I'll highlight it for you. Do you see the next date on 45 --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: 4547, it's the 17th, correct, 95, do you see that on the top? You had it just a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And then there is 14 conversations that are captured on the 17th of July, and then you see an entry of the 18th of July; correct? Which is on 0080-4557.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And then there is nine conversations for that day. And if you look at 0080-4564, 4565 I'm sorry, we have the date of the 19th of July, 1995; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And it goes on and on with every date specifically. But we could look at it, I don't think it's necessarily -- necessary to see it there. You'll see that there is a nine conversations for the 19th, seven conversations, sir, for the 20th of July, ten conversations, sir, for the 21st of July, then we have a date missing, approximately the 22nd of July, then an entry for the 23rd of July where there are 15 entries of conversations that were purportedly captured, and the book ends there. My specific question to you, sir, before we break is: Can you tell me why during the period of the 11th through the 16th, why there were so few conversations when it seems that you averaged from the 16th through the -- what did I say, was it the 24th? The 16th through the 23rd of July, there were 96 conversations captured in that one-week period. So I want to take the same one-week period. How can you differentiate that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I can just give you an assumption. I don't remember the exact period and those days, but based on my experience, based on my previous knowledge and work in that unit, I can even give you some assumptions that might be very close to the truth. Something that I believe would be true but I don't know how good that is for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, I always believe in the truth, sir, and -- but it's not my decision to allow you to answer or not to answer a question that you say may be speculative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll decide to what extent at all it is speculative, in which case we will just eradicate it. So, yes, please, sir, Witness, could you try to give us your explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There could be several reasons in my view. It is possible that there were a lot of irrelevant conversations that we did not to write in the notebook. It's possible. I don't know how important the other intercepts were. I didn't read them. Had I read them, then I would have told you, Well, listen this intercept is worthless. There was no need to record it. But I didn't read them, so I can't tell you. So that's one possible reason. The other possible reason is that on their side, there was some movement of radio equipment, that they had a new organisation, new elevation or something, and that that caused a delay. This is something that I can assume based on my experience. I don't really have a third reason. I just gave you these two assumptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. But I can -- sir, looking again just immediately before the break, one last question, and this is very straightforward. Do you see on page -- or on the logbook, 0080-43 -- strike that, 0080-4537, where we saw the date 16.7.95 placed in there? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting above this entry? Is that your handwriting immediately above 16.7.95?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes. I can recognise my hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Is that your handwriting immediately above that? At 12.15?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And how about the conversation below, sir? Is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sir, who wrote 16.7.95 on this page; do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: This is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sir, why would you write 16.7.95 to start the next day of a conversation that you did not listen to or capture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Sometimes, if I were the last one to record something before the new shift came in, as I was about to finish my shift, for example, if it was 10.00 p.m. or 12.00 p.m., if I was the last operator working at the equipment, I had this habit of putting the date, just in order to show that this was one shift and a new one was coming. That's my explanation, because I don't think that what follows after this date was written by somebody from my team because I simply don't recognise the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we can take the break now, I think it's the right time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a 25-minute break or did we have any redactions this time? 25 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to have to interpose my learned friend's cross-examination, but various members of our team have been trying to sort out the provisional release of our client, and at one point in time I thought I was going to be applying for a different airport for him to depart from the Netherlands. But it now transpires that the government of Serbia, who have been helpful and cooperative with our team, are unable to fly General Gvero out of the Netherlands on the 19th of December. We had assumed, and this is why we withdrew the motion that we filed a day or two ago, that special arrangements were being made for our client to leave this country on that day. We have just been told that that is now not possible. We therefore, Your Honour, with regret, have to resurrect the motion that we withdrew two days ago and ask that he be released a day earlier, on the 18th of December and he will leave by scheduled airplane via Schiphol airport. Mr. Krgovic spoke briefly to my learned friend Mr. McCloskey about it and I understand he doesn't object, but I have to say we literally just told him because we literally just learned ourselves of the present position. I'm sorry about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's your duty, Mr. Josse. You needn't be sorry about this. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No problem, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to dispose of the resurrected motion. And having heard your submissions and also the no objection registered by the Prosecution, we are hereby granting the motion orally. Madam Registrar, since we are short of time, please communicate this, our oral decision, to the various persons concerned, various authorities concerned. Last but not least, to the Dutch authorities, because they need to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are grateful to the Trial Chamber and of course the registry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Mr. Ostojic, you will wait a little bit until we get the witness in. We are obviously not going to finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, Your Honour, it doesn't look like it and I feel bad for everyone, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The evidence of this witness concerns your client more than anybody else, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sir, hi again. I was unclear on your last answer that you gave us, and we are talking about the intercept page 0080-4537, where you wrote in the date 16 July 1995. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, you told us, sir, that if you were the last operator working at the equipment, and this is on page 72, lines 19 through 21: "I had this habit of putting the date just to -- just in order to show that this was one shift and a new one was coming." You remember that? You just said it a half hour ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, do you know, sir, since you used the word habit, did you do it on each and every occasion that your shift ended or on just this one occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I think that this was the only time that I was the last operator before a new shift. I couldn't do it each time. It depended on the schedule of the shifts. I couldn't be the last one each time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, on page 72 again, on line 19, you say if it was 10.00 p.m. or 12.00 p.m. then you were in the habit of writing this date. Sir, the intercept immediately above the 16th of July, 1995, is it your testimony that that's 12.15 midnight, or 12.15 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I meant that it was noon, 100 per cent, because if it was midnight then it would have said 00. That was about the time that the shift changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this, then, if the shift changes mid-day, what's the necessity to put the date at that time? What I'm asking you, sir, how did you know in advance that there were going to be no other conversations for the remainder of that day, from 12.00 in the afternoon until what seems to be the next conversation that was captured at 9.45 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I put the date in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He's already answered the question. I just was going to ask for a rephrase given the nature of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he understood it, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sir, if you could look to the front of this book, and we have a copy but you have the original, if you could close the book to your right. Now do you see what's in the middle of that book, after the word Papo city LI, and then there is something else that's on this book, do you see that, 1 GEN period 2001. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: It's in blue -- blue ink, I think.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Can you, sir, by looking at the original there, can you determine whether or not that was stamped on there, whether it was taped on there, or did it originally have that information on the book when it was initially manufactured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I think that it's 100 per cent written when the notebook was produced. When the notebook was produced, that's when it was done. We couldn't have done this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And, sir, there is another similar description like that on the right-hand side immediately above that, I think it's in green ink, is it not, see it on the right-hand side, right? If you don't mind just putting that on the ELMO or if the Court would allow the usher to help him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Are you thinking of this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: It's the same thing. When the notebook was produced. It's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. That's helpful, thank you. Sir, I went through your notebook and tried to identify some of your signatures. There is no other entry that I found, sir, which remotely suggests that you ever heard Mr. Beara's voice. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If there could be a time frame provided for that question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Spring of 1995 up until the time he left the southern facility, as we call it, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you understand the question, Witness? Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's just that I believe the question was tied to the notebook, so it's just a little incongruous, that's all. If I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I think we are beyond the notebook. We have his testimony on that issue. I was asking him now on the frequency in which he purports to have heard Mr. Beara's voice, so it's a totally different issue. Maybe I should highlight that when I ask a different group of questions. It's a totally different issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're suggesting to him that he was not correct in his previous answers that he had heard Beara's voice on several occasions by referring him to the entries in this notebook. That's how I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, or any notebook, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it was -- there is no entry that I found in referring to that notebook that he has in front of him that would remotely suggest that he ever heard Mr. Beara's voice to. So if you are referring -- you want to refer him also to other notebooks you need to be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We will, but we'll take it maybe one notebook at a time and maybe I can just summarise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then I was right, you were referring to this notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Could you please put the question to me again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: In looking at this notebook, 22 I think it's identified as, number 22, I couldn't find any conversation that you purportedly recorded which bears a conversation that was captured which included Mr. Beara. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Well, if you look through it, then you are 100 per cent right, if -- as far as the intercepts are concerned. If there aren't any, then there aren't any. If Beara's name doesn't appear, then it means he doesn't appear. If you would like to know now how many times I heard him in that period when he began to appear, I mean, I don't understand what you are asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking, sir, to know approximately the frequency in which you claim to have heard Mr. Beara's voice. According to the notebook, this one, and any other notebook for that matter, I couldn't find with respect to your handwritten intercepted conversations any reference that you captured a conversation which included Mr. Beara. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: You're correct, but that doesn't necessarily mean that I didn't hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: In fact, sir, I couldn't find any conversations that you claim to have recorded or captured, I should say, involving Mr. Beara before or after the 16th of July 1995, in any of the notebooks. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: If you were unable to find them, then it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting to you, sir, is not that I couldn't find them. They just simply don't exist; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: If he's not there, then they don't exist. I'm interested in exactly what you would like to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And I'll ask the question. Thank you for your patience on that. Sir, the OTP never showed you any other intercepts which purport to involve Mr. Beara, did they? Yours or by any other intercept operator; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, let me show you book 231, which has, I think, the Exhibit number P02315 on the e-court, please. And if we can turn to the page with the ERN number 01077918.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Could you please rotate the image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... while we are -- while they are rotating it, sir, the 16th of July, 1995 seems to be written in in several books. Can I ask you this? Although I don't know that this book is directly related to you or this southern site, do you know if you wrote in there that you see in the middle of the page, 16.07.95 in this book as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No means that you didn't?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did not write this down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, who wrote the 14.07.95 right above that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: According to this, sir, although it may not have your handwriting on it, there -- this is the beginning of a new day, the 14th of July, correct, and the beginning of a new day, the 16th of July, 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Just so I understand these books correctly, hopefully, there was apparently no conversation in this book recorded for the 14th of July and no conversation in this book that was recorded whatsoever on the 15th of July, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sir, I want to direct your attention to a different point so that we could all follow along, and I know you don't remember dates specifically or -- specifically. Sir, when the fall of Srebrenica occurred on approximately or on or about the 10th of July, 1995, did you or any of your intercept operators discuss where the people from Srebrenica were going? Were you able to pick up any such conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Probably we did have such conversations, but I don't remember them. Right now, I wouldn't be able to repeat back for you a single sentence from that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And it would be found, if anywhere, it would be found in these logbooks; correct? Specifically let's say the 8th or the 9th in preparation of the enclave falling and then immediately thereafter, the 11th, 12th and so on, it would be found in those notebooks. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I understand the question well, I think that really calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not necessarily. That's our decision. If in answering he -- we notice that he's speculating, then obviously we will stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And only if he knows, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. And it doesn't necessarily follow that in answering this question he needs to speculate. Let's -- so let's answer this question, Witness. Perhaps you can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'll try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if, in the intercept books that you reviewed in preparation for your testimony, do you know if the events prior to the fall of Srebrenica would have been included in these notebooks, the preparation for the fall of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The way you have phrased it, if I were answering the question, I would have told you it's confusing but --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll ask the exact question. I just have to find it here, Judge. I'm sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I stated this, and I'll just read the question again. Thank you for your patience. Would it be found anywhere in these logbooks specifically let's say the 8th, or the 9th in preparation of the enclave falling, and then immediately thereafter, the 11th, 12th and so on, it would be found in those notebooks; correct? Any conversations that you may have captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "You" in the singular, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but -- yes. And then I was going to ask him plural, but I didn't want to get an objection for compound but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, I don't know anything about this notebook. I've never seen it before and I don't know who wrote this in. I'm only talking about my own notebook, if I can. And as for my own notebook, all I can say is one thing: We wrote what we heard. We didn't write unimportant things. That's one thing. But about what was in there, should there have been anything about the preparations there or anything like that, I really don't know. I mean, it wasn't my job to think about these things. I was doing this job the way we were doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, what do you define your job as being, sir, at that time, July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: My job was to replace the shift that was before me, if that was possible, because of the weather and everything, and then to make a schedule of work amongst our people, to stick to as much as I was able, to the schedule, to intercept conversations, if the scanners found them or the antennas found them, to try to record that and to try to transcribe it into the notebook, then to try with the guy who was doing it to send it, sometimes to make lunch or bread, to rest when I was tired, again to wait for the next shift and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: If I can just interrupt you, I wasn't quite asking that detail. I'll put the question to you, sir. Specifically wasn't one of the tasks that you were given in July of 1995 was to listen in on the various VRS officers and military personnel in order to assist in the defence of the Srebrenica enclave? Wasn't that one of your tasks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: The task had to do not only with the Srebrenica enclave but anything that could help at any side. Whatever channel we heard something on, it needn't necessarily have been the Srebrenica channel, we would transcribe and send off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Transcribe listening to conversations of whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Conversations of those people that our scanner found. Sometimes they were not military personnel. On those channels you could sometimes hear civilian conversations. I guess they had that option, the army of Republika Srpska, to connect civilians for telephone conversations. I listened to a couple of civilians. How they connected them I don't know, but we even sometimes managed to listen in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sir, if you can go back to that book and turn to that page or perhaps with the assistance of the usher, with the Court's permission, 0080-4537 again and they will help you. Actually, the book to your right, the logbook, 4537. Again, I just want to make sure, it's your handwriting that's denoted as being 16 July 1995. Immediately above that there is an entry of an intercept timed 12.15 in the afternoon; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have it placed on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And, again, I'm not sure if I got your answer correctly, because I know you were talking when I said "above that." That intercept, sir, is that an intercept that you captured and you wrote down? In other words, it that your handwriting at 12.15?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, I said that before too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And when, sir, would your shifts end then? At midnight on the day when they ended or at a different hour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Our shifts changed approximately at noon. When the crew set off, sometimes they would come at 10.00 in the morning, sometimes they would come at noon. Sometimes they would be a couple of hours late because they had to bring water, because there was a shortage of water. I couldn't give you an exact hour. It varied. But in any case, it was definitely during the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So what time did your shift end on the 15th of July, 1995? Do you know by looking at this page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I don't know if my shift ended on the 15th of July. I don't know if it ended on the 15th of July. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You wrote the entry the 16th of July 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and I think your testimony, sir, was that it was the habit at the end of your shift to write the date for the next shift; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: If I was the last operator I used to do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And it looks by this, because it's apparently your handwriting, you were the last operator at noon on the 16th or 15th of 1995 [sic], sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes. That possibility exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: What I want to know about this conversation on 12.15, this conversation is really a conversation that occurred on the 16th of July, 1995, and after you wrote that conversation apparently there was a switch or a change in shifts, and that you wrote the date right underneath that; correct? Otherwise, sir, it really wouldn't make sense why at noon you would have written the next day what the date was because you couldn't have been clairvoyant and found that there would be no conversations whatsoever from noon until midnight.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Again, I say I can only give you the answer that I gave earlier why this was done, I cannot speculate further. I gave an answer why I would have written something like that. It was a custom. I don't know what would have been the reason. It would be speculation. So I cannot give you 100 per cent definite explanation. I would really like to go back to that time, but I really cannot. It was too long ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sir, if we can flip --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, please. Can we see the previous page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not the previous. The previous, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Maybe the usher can assist, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, we need to zoom out first.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think the Court would like to see 4536 but also 4535 [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, the 16th of July appears on the last four numbers of the ERN 4537. I think the Court would like to see 4536 and then also 4535.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to 4534 first. I can't see any dates there. And the previous page. And the previous page, 4532.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may just help Your Honour, I think we had indicated and I think the Prosecutor is in agreement the only date that appears before that is the 11th of July on 4528.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- see the previous pages to make sure that there are no dates indicated. Yes, we can go to 4536 now. This is page you wanted us to look at, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, actually 45 -- strike that. Let me start again. The prior page, which is 4535, which starts the conversation of an intercept at 10.00. You should look at both pages, I would suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Okay. And the next 4536? I suppose it's a continuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It seems to be, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. 4537 is where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Your question, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sir, given now that we've established that your shifts changed at approximately noon or thereabouts and that you ended your shift on that date and then entered this date of 16 July 1995, am I correct that the conversations that precede that, namely the one at 12.15 in the afternoon and the one immediately before that at 10.00 a.m., occurred purportedly on the 16th of July, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: If I wrote in that date when it was supposed to be, then that should have meant that. I explained about the date already. The date was added, possibly added, when we were leaving but again, these are all possibilities. I never said that was so and that was so. It's possible when I was last in the shift as we were leaving that I would write it down. It's possible. I cannot tell you precisely what I did 11 years ago. I did mention that as a possibility, but please don't hold me to that date. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sir, but given your testimony, isn't it more likely than not, and isn't it certain that as you've testified when your shift ended you made this notation of 16 July 1995, that in fact, that was the date that those conversations were captured, if at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: No. You asserted that, that that was that intercept written in on that day. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. We'll go back and study your testimony carefully on that point. Sir, did you know, you specifically, and your group, because we are running a little short of time so if I could just be given the latitude to ask a somewhat compound question, did you or your men, sir, know that the people from Srebrenica were going to Potocari on or about the 10th or 11th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: At the time, we probably knew, but I cannot remember now if we did or didn't. At the time, we knew much of what was going on, but that was a while ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And I understand that. And, sir, those are important events, were they not, for you to capture any conversations that you may have heard and to transmit those conversations to your superiors; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And, sir, did you know or your men know that there was screening of enemy combatants that were being conducted in Potocari during that same period, the 12th through the 15th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Again, as I say, if we did get something in a dispatch, then we probably assumed something at that time but I really couldn't say now. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, do you know, sir, that these some enemy military combatants were being interrogated at Potocari in what was defined as an interrogation house? Did you ever learn about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, number 1, I think he's answered that question. It's been slightly rephrased, but I think it's essentially the same question, and I think we are beginning to get a little far afield of the subject matter of this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry about that. Objection sustained. I think you need to restrict to what this witness came here to testify about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sir, could we look at that intercept 4535, please? Do you see it on tab 1 in your book? You can look at the copy that the Prosecutor gave you or the original, whichever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now looking at the original book, sir, do you see that in certain portions of this two-page conversation -- or two and a half page conversation that you captured, allegedly, do you see that the period is somewhat highlighted and that apparently someone who wrote the period made it a little darker than the balance of the text? Do you see that in the original? Perhaps it's easier to see it in the original, which is to your right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I see that the time is indicated as 1000 in just plain figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sir, can you look at the original book to your right, which is on the ELMO? And we'll take it page by page. The first page of the conversation is at 4535. Do you see that? Now, do you see anywhere there, sir, in the original, although we don't have the benefit of looking at it but you can look at it, where a period ending a sentence of a purported conversation is actually highlighted more than just a little bit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Which sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, if you look through the first one, the second one, the fourth one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Is that the way you made your period, sir, a little larger and a little darker than just the dot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Well, just depends. Sometimes I write it like this, sometimes I write it like that, the dot or the period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let's see the next page, sir, 4536, please. The top of that page, I think you can see, there seems to be some numbers that come before 0080. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: 8, 8, well, there is something coming through from the other side. I just see that there are seals from the other side coming through before 00804. I just see that the seal on the opposite side was such a strong impression that it sort of leaked through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. It bled through; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, from the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, sir, focusing on the beginning part of that conversation, I want to take the first four entries that you make and we'll break this down one at a time where it starts with B, K, B and K; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, sir, Mr. Thayer mentioned in his summary that another portion of this conversation was captured by some other units. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: When you write the time down, do you write the time that you initially begin capturing the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So can you tell us, sir, how many minutes after these other units supposedly picked up this conversation, that you were able to pick up the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I can't tell you how many minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, do you remember, sir, in the Krstic case, that you were asked that it was a three-minute differential between some other intercept and your intercept; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you don't remember or -- I know it's possible but that's what you said and that's what it reflects. But we'll move on in the interests of time. I don't think there is an argument about it, quite frankly. Sir, can you tell me in this intercept that you captured on these two and a half pages, how many times does purportedly General Krstic refer to Ljubo Beara by his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Hmm, I would have to go over it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me do it, because I did it just in the interests of time, if I may, and since it is cross-examination. There is no reference whatsoever by General Krstic of Mr. Beara by his last name; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I would have to check that too. If you checked it, I trust you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I appreciate that very much. Sir, the only time that General Krstic purportedly identifies the person he's speaking to is by his first name, Ljubo, on three occasions; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I need to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You're welcome to do that or you can trust me or maybe you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I'll trust you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I do appreciate that, sir, very much. Sir, again focusing on the first four entries, B, K, and then B, K, again, I want to look at the last section there where you put the entry for K, you put Fasica and Sladojevic; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Yes, Tasica or Sladojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, on my copy it looked like an F, so, yes, Tasica, and then the next person is Sladojevic, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know, sir, whether Mr. Sladojevic was a colonel at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: Hmm, I don't remember Sladojevic at all right now. I don't remember him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, whether or not he was in the Main Staff at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I just don't remember Sladojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, if at that time, July of 1995, you and the other intercept operators had a dossier or a printed form identifying various individuals that was given to you by your command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: I personally don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you, sir, that you never had such a dossier. Would I be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133
utterances.text: If that is your position, perhaps, but I gave you my answer. My answer is I don't remember that. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's fair. Thank you. That's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have a couple areas left, just to go through the transcript. Maybe 25 minutes, Your Honour, tomorrow. I'm just letting the Court know because I know I'm approaching the two-hour mark according to what I've been advised, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And more or less the time indicated by the other Defence teams remains the same? Anyway, we have to stop now. We will continue tomorrow morning, as it looks, we'll probably be over with this witness's testimony during the first session. And then unless there is some kind of business to transact, we will -- we can then safely adjourn. Before we adjourn, I just want -- Mr. Josse, I just wanted to make sure, in relation to the decision, all right. So that there is no misunderstanding, we are sticking to the date of the return of your client. That will remain the 27th?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, please, because in fact, we have been informed there is no flight, direct flight on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, I'm making it clear for everyone and for the record that he will leave on the 18th instead of the 19th and he will return as per our decision on the 27th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's our application, and we would be very grateful, as I've already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Thank you. So we stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.
